title: What Did Early Humans Actually Do at Night? | Cozy History for Sleep
description: Settle in for a slow, gentle journey back forty thousand years, to one long night with a small band of Ice Age families. We follow them from the last light of the afternoon, through cooking, firelight, stories, the deep quiet of the small hours, and on to a cold grey dawn. Calm narration, hand-drawn scenes, and nothing to startle you. Made to be listened to with your eyes closed.

sources.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History - What does it mean to be human? (Human Evolution Evidence)

topic: What did early humans actually do at night?

beats.say: Before we begin, get comfortable. Let your shoulders drop, and let the pillow take the weight of your head. There is nothing you need to do for the next couple of hours. Tonight we are going a very long way back, to a time before cities, before farms, before anyone had ever written a word. We are going to spend one long night with a small group of people who lived about forty thousand years ago, during the last great Ice Age. They are walking home now, along the river, as the light begins to go.

There are perhaps twenty or thirty of them in all. A few families who have lived and travelled together for as long as anyone can remember. The man in front carries a bundle of dry branches on his shoulder. The woman beside him has a basket of roots and berries gathered through the afternoon. Nobody hurries. The evening air is cool and smells of river water and woodsmoke, and the low sun turns everything the colour of honey.

Their home, for this season at least, is the mouth of a wide, shallow cave in a limestone hillside. It faces south, so it catches the sun for most of the day, and the rock above keeps off the rain. An old man sits near the entrance, exactly where he has sat for most of the afternoon, and a girl waves as the gatherers come into view. A fire has been burning here, small and steady, since morning.

People like these did not usually live deep inside caves. The deep chambers were dark, damp and cold. What they wanted was the entrance: light, air, a view of the valley, and a roof of stone. Archaeologists find the traces of their fires, their tools, and their meals right here, at the front, where the daylight reaches. Sometimes they built a screen of branches and hides across the opening, to keep out the wind. Tonight the air is still, and the screen is not needed.

The world outside is colder than the one you know. Great sheets of ice lie far to the north, and the summers are short. But the land is not empty. It is rich with grass, and the grass feeds enormous herds: horses, reindeer, bison, and further off, the slow, shaggy mammoths. A hunter pauses on the slope with his spear and points. Somewhere below, a deer has lifted its head to listen. The child beside him watches, and says nothing.

Back at the cave, the woman with the basket kneels and begins to sort what she has found. Roots go in one pile, berries in another. A few good flat stones, picked up on the way, go by the fire. Her child copies her, moving pebbles from one heap to the next with great seriousness. This is how a great deal of learning happened in a world without schools: by watching, by copying, and by being allowed to help.

Down at the river, a little way from the cave, one of the men is still fishing. He stands very still in the shallows, and the water slides past his shins, cold and clear. Behind him, on a frame of sticks, a few fish caught earlier are already drying in the smoke of a small fire. He will give it a little longer. The best fish, he knows, come in the last light of the day.

Two others are at the water's edge, filling skin bags and a wooden bowl. Water is the first thing any camp needs, and carrying it home before dark is one of the evening's quiet jobs. The girl has a bowl in her hands and is trying not to spill it. She spills a little. Nobody minds. The river is wide and slow here, and it goes on murmuring to itself as the sky turns from gold to rose.

One by one, the people come home. The wood carrier drops his bundle by the fire with a soft thud. The fisherman arrives with a string of fish. The water carriers set down their bags. Nobody counts heads out loud, but everybody notices who is back and who is not. A small band like this lives by keeping track of one another. By the time the sun touches the far hills, they are nearly all here, and the fire has been fed.

The old man looks up at the first star. It is faint, and very high, and he has seen it appear on ten thousand evenings just like this one. He does not know what a star is. He does not need to. He knows that this one comes before the others, and that when it is joined by three more, the night has properly begun. The child beside him looks up too, and finds it, and is pleased.

The last person home is the hunter from the slope. He comes back without the deer. That is how most evenings end for a hunter: not with a kill, but with a long walk and a story about what nearly happened. Meat came to camp perhaps once or twice in a week, and when it did, it was shared. Tonight there are fish, and roots, and berries, and that is enough. He leans his spear against the rock, and sits down by the fire, and the night settles in around them.

There is always a little more to do while there is still light to do it by. A woman sits with a lump of flint in her lap and a smooth round stone in her hand, and taps, and turns the flint, and taps again. Each tap sends a thin, sharp flake skittering onto the hide spread in front of her. These flakes are knives. In a few minutes she has made half a dozen, each one sharper than anything in your kitchen drawer. The girl beside her collects the flakes carefully, by their blunt ends.

Nearby, a man is sewing. His needle is a sliver of bone, polished smooth, with a tiny hole drilled through one end. His thread is sinew, the tough fibre from a deer's leg, softened in his mouth. He is closing a seam in a fur boot, and he works slowly, pushing the needle through a hole he has already made with a stone awl. Needles like his have been found in caves across Europe and Asia. They are one of the reasons people could live at all in a world this cold.

On the wooden frame beside the cave, hides are stretched to dry. A deer hide, scraped clean on the inside, becomes a blanket, or a sleeping mat, or a bag, or part of a tent. Nothing from an animal was wasted if it could be helped. The child points at the biggest hide and says something, and the woman laughs. Perhaps it was a joke. Forty thousand years is a long time, and we do not know what they found funny. But we can be sure that they laughed.

Two more are coming in from the far side of the valley with the last of the firewood. In a landscape like this, with few trees, wood was precious, and gathering it took a long part of every day. They carried dead branches, dry grass, and dung from the herds, which burns slowly and well. The old man walking with a stick has been out with them all afternoon. He is slower than he was, but he knows where the good wood lies, and that knowledge is worth a great deal.

The cooking fire is tended now with more care. Flat stones have been pushed into the embers to heat. A woman crouches and stirs a wooden bowl of water with a stick, and in a moment she will drop a hot stone into it, and the water will hiss and steam. This is how you boil water when you have no pot that can sit in a flame. It works surprisingly well. Roots go into the hot water and slowly soften. A man nearby is already eating a handful of berries, because he cannot wait, and nobody stops him.

Down by the river, the girl who spilled the water sits alone for a moment on the bank. She is watching the clouds turn purple and the water turn silver. Children in a band like this were rarely truly alone, and rarely far from an adult. But there were moments like this one, at the edges of the day, when a child could sit with her own thoughts and the sound of the river. Then someone calls her name, and she gets up, and walks back toward the light of the fire.

There is a great deal of talking as the day winds down. Where the herds are moving. Which of the berry bushes are nearly finished. Whose feet are sore. Who saw the tracks of a bear by the stream, and how old the tracks were. These conversations were not idle. They were how the band kept its map of the world up to date, and everyone, even the children, had something to add. The old man on his log listens more than he speaks. He has heard most of it before.

The hunter sits with his spear across his knees and checks the point. It is a slim blade of flint, bound to the shaft with sinew and glue made from boiled birch bark. He runs his thumb along the edge, and nods. Tomorrow he will go out again, and the spear must be right. He does not resent the deer that got away. There will be other deer. In a world where you could not store much food, patience was not a virtue. It was simply how you lived.

The smallest child has already fallen asleep, curled against his mother on a bed of dry grass and fur. He was awake before the sun, and he has walked a long way today on short legs. His mother does not move him. She sits with one hand resting on his back, and looks at the fire, and lets the tiredness of the day come over her too. Nobody tells small children when to sleep in a camp like this. They sleep when they are tired, where they are, and someone keeps them warm.

Out on the grass, two of the men stand looking north, toward the mountains, where the clouds have gathered. They are reading the weather. The old man points with his stick and says a few words, and the younger one nods. It will rain in the night, perhaps, or it will not. Either way, they know it now, and they walk back to tell the others. The last of the light drains out of the sky behind them, and the fire, which was one light among many all day, becomes the only light there is.

Now the night has truly come, and the fire is the centre of everything. A man crouches beside it and feeds it, one branch at a time, laying each piece just so. He is not building a bonfire. A big fire wastes wood, and wood is precious. He wants a small, steady, hot fire that will burn all night with a little attention, and give heat and light and a thin curl of smoke that keeps the biting insects away. He has done this every night of his life. His hands know the work without him.

People had been keeping fires for a very, very long time before this night. Hundreds of thousands of years, perhaps more. By now, making a new fire was a skill, and keeping an old one alive was a habit. The old man tells the child, as old men did, that once, long ago, people did not have fire at all, and had to eat their food cold and sleep in the dark. The child cannot imagine it. Neither, honestly, can the old man. But it makes a good story.

If the fire ever did go out, they could make another. One way was to strike a lump of iron-rich stone against a sharp flint, and catch the sparks in a nest of dry fungus or shredded bark. Another was to spin a dry stick fast against a dry board until the dust it made began to smoulder. Both ways took skill, and patience, and dry tinder, which was the hardest thing to find on a wet night. So the easiest way of all was simply never to let the fire go out.

When a band moved camp, someone carried the fire with them. A glowing coal, packed in moss or dry dung inside a hollow horn or a bundle of bark, could be kept alive for hours of walking. When they stopped, they blew on it, fed it, and the fire that had warmed them last night warmed them again tonight, in a new place. Some fires, in this way, may have burned for years, or lifetimes. Nobody kept count.

The hot stones are lifted from the fire now with two sticks, and dropped one after another into the wooden bowl. The water leaps and hisses. The roots inside it, tough and starchy, begin to soften and sweeten. A man beside the cook has started on the fish, which were laid on the flat stones at the edge of the fire and are crisp and smoky. There is no hurry, and no plates, and no one goes without. Food, in a camp like this, belonged to everybody.

The old man eats slowly, because his teeth are worn, and because there is no reason to eat fast. He has lived a long time for his world, perhaps fifty years, perhaps more. His knees ache and his eyes are not what they were, but he can still tell every story the band has, and he knows where every spring is for three days' walk in any direction. The child sharing his fish does not think of him as old. She thinks of him as the one who knows things.

So they eat, all of them, in a loose ring around the fire. Faces flicker orange and gold. Behind them, beyond the firelight, the valley is very dark and very large. The smell of smoke and fish and the sweet, earthy steam of the cooking roots drifts out into it. Somewhere in that darkness, animals are moving, and the people know it, and are not afraid. The fire is between them and the night, and it has always been enough.

Afterwards, the woman who cooked gathers up the bones and the fish skins and the peelings, and carries them a little way off, away from the sleeping place. Rubbish that stays where you sleep brings flies, and smells, and worse. Archaeologists find these little rubbish heaps, thousands of years later, and read them like a diary: what was eaten, in what season, and how it was cooked. Tonight's diary entry is short. Fish. Roots. Berries. A good day.

The fire is fed again, and settles. Two people sit close to it with their hands out, palms to the flames, the way people have sat by fires since there were fires to sit by. The cold has come down with the dark, and the stone of the cave is cool at their backs, and the warmth on their faces and hands feels like a kindness. Nobody says anything for a while. They watch the flames, and the flames do what flames do, and that is enough to watch.

A little way inside the cave, a second, smaller fire has been lit, where the sleeping furs are laid out. The old man has moved there, out of the draught, and two of the children have followed him. Above them, on the pale rock of the wall, are the shapes of animals, painted in red earth by someone a long time ago: a horse, a bison, a row of dots that might be a count of something. In the firelight, they seem to move. The children have seen them every night of their lives, and still they look.

The fire keeper lights a torch from the flames, a bundle of resinous wood, and goes to check the edge of the camp before the night grows late. He is not looking for anything in particular. He is looking at everything, the way you might check the doors of a house before bed. The firewood is stacked. The hides are on their frame. The water bags are full and hung from a branch. He comes back, pushes the torch into the ground beside the fire, and sits. The night is theirs now, and they have hours of it to spend.

You might think that when the sun went down, the work stopped. It did not, quite. The firelight is not as good as daylight, but it is good enough for the small, close jobs, and there is time now that there was not during the day. A woman sits with a piece of hide across her knees and stitches, slowly, a row of tiny holes and a line of sinew. She is making a hood. Winter is coming, and the wind off the ice does not care how tired you are.

Beside her, a man works on a spear point. He holds the flint against a pad of leather in his palm and presses the tip of an antler against its edge, and a thin flake lifts away with a soft click. Press, click. Press, click. Each flake makes the edge a little sharper and the point a little thinner. This is slow, careful work, and firelight is enough for it, because his fingers can feel what his eyes cannot quite see. A good point might take him most of the evening. He has most of the evening.

The old man watches the flint worker and, from time to time, says something. Turn it. Not there. Yes, there. He was the best maker of points in the band once, and his hands remember, even if they shake a little now. Skills like this passed from the old to the young over thousands of evenings like this one, by watching, by trying, by being corrected gently, and by trying again. There was no other way to learn, and no other school.

A little further in, where the second fire burns, a woman is weaving. Not cloth; that will not come for thousands of years yet. She is twisting plant fibres into cord, rolling them against her thigh, then twisting two cords together into something stronger. Cord like this tied spear points to shafts, hung bags from branches, strung beads, and held the whole camp together. The girl beside her holds the loose end and keeps it from tangling. It is a small job, and she does it well.

Another man is doing something less useful, and more important. He has a small, flat pebble in his hand, and with the point of a flint he is scratching a shape into it: a few lines, curving, that might be the back of a horse, or a bison, or nothing at all. He tilts it to the firelight to see. The child leaning against him watches the lines appear, and gasps a little when the shape becomes an animal. People were making pictures like this, on stone and bone and cave walls, all through this age. Nobody is sure why. Perhaps for the same reason you would.

A woman crosses the firelight with an armful of dry grass for the sleeping place. Beds in a camp like this were thick layers of grass and bracken with hides laid over them, and they were remade often, because grass flattens and gets damp and fills with small crawling things. Fresh bedding was one of the pleasures of an evening. She lays it down inside the cave, near the second fire, and shakes out the furs over it, and the smell of dry grass drifts back out to where the others sit.

Someone passes a skin bag of water, and someone drinks. There is no beer yet, and no wine. Those will wait for farming, and farming is thirty thousand years away. What people drank was water, cold from the river, and sometimes, in the right season, the sweet juice of crushed berries, or a tea of leaves steeped in a bowl of water heated with stones. Whether it did anything, nobody knew. But it tasted of summer, and that was reason enough.

The girl has been given a bowl of the crushed berries, and she holds it in both hands and drinks slowly, to make it last. It is deep red, and sweet, and a little sour. She has purple all round her mouth. Her mother tells her something, and she nods, and wipes her face with the back of her hand, which makes it worse. Some things about children have not changed in forty thousand years, and probably will not change in forty thousand more.

The fire keeper straightens a spear shaft. He has cut a young, straight sapling, stripped the bark, and now he warms it, section by section, over the coals, and then bends it gently against his knee to take the curve out. Wood heated this way will hold a new shape when it cools. He sights along it, one eye closed, the way a carpenter sights along a plank, and warms it again. The smell of hot green wood joins the smell of the smoke.

And so the evening goes on, quietly. The sewer sews. The flint worker presses and clicks. The old man nods, and his chin drops toward his chest, and he catches himself, and nods again. The smallest child sleeps through all of it on his bed of grass. There is no clock, and there is nowhere to be. When the work is done, or the eyes are too tired to do it, it stops. And that time is coming closer now, as the fire burns down toward its red heart.

The older children are not ready for sleep. They rarely are. A girl and a boy have found a game near the edge of the firelight, something to do with a stick and a stone and a great deal of running back and forth. The grown-ups glance up now and then, and go back to their work. Children in a band like this grew up inside a circle of adults, all of whom kept half an eye on them, and none of whom fussed very much. Bumps and scrapes were part of the evening.

When the game tires them out, they come to the old man, because the old man has stories. He does not tell them the way you might read a book. He tells them the way he was told, with his hands moving and his voice going up and down, and pauses in the right places so that the children lean in. Tonight it is the story of the hunter who followed a reindeer for three days and came home with nothing but a good story, which the children like, because the hunter in the story is sitting right over there, and pretending not to listen.

The girl points up at the painted horse on the cave wall and asks who made it. The old man says, honestly, that he does not know. It was there when he was a boy, and it was old then. Perhaps his grandmother's people. Perhaps people before them. Across this whole age, people painted and carved and scratched, and most of what they made is gone. What is left, on the walls of deep caves, is the smallest part of it. The girl looks at the horse for a long time.

A boy of perhaps eight has been given a real piece of flint and a real hammerstone, and is trying to make a flake. His mother sits beside him and does not help, except to move his thumb once, out of the way. He hits the flint and nothing happens. He hits it again, and a flake jumps off, crooked and thick, and he holds it up in triumph. It is not a good flake. It is his first. She tells him so, and he keeps it.

Children in this world worked, in their way. They carried firewood and water, gathered berries, picked the shells and bones out of the rubbish for beads and toys, and looked after children smaller than themselves. But they also played, all the time, at everything. They played at hunting with little spears, and at cooking with little bowls, and at being the old man with a stick and a croaky voice, which made everyone laugh, including the old man.

The hunter, who has been pretending not to listen, finally joins in, and tells the end of the story his own way, with the reindeer much bigger and much cleverer than the old man made it. The children know they are being teased and do not care. This is how a band remembered itself. Every hunt, every move of camp, every hard winter and lucky summer became a story, and the stories were told and told again until everyone knew them, and could tell them to their own children.

The girl is given a last drink of water, and yawns hugely in the middle of it. Her mother takes the bowl before it spills. It is late for the children, though nobody here would say so, or could say what "late" meant. Children slept when they were tired. They slept near their parents and grandparents and cousins, in a heap of furs and grass and warm bodies, and if they woke in the night they were never alone, and never in the dark, because the fire was always there.

So the girl is led inside to the bed of fresh grass, and she lies down, and her mother sits beside her for a minute and talks quietly, about nothing, the way you might. The girl's eyes are already closed. On the wall above her, the painted horse stands in its red earth, as it has stood for longer than anyone remembers. The fire clicks. The smell of the new grass is sweet. And she is asleep before her mother has finished the sentence.

The boy with the flake is still awake, just, sitting against his father's knee by the fire with the flake held tight in his fist. He is fighting sleep the way children do, and losing. His father does not send him to bed. There is no bed to send him to, really, only the furs, and he will get there. In a while, his father will simply lift him, still holding the flake, and carry him in, and lay him down, and he will not wake until the grey of the morning.

And that is what happens. The boy is lifted and carried. The sewing woman looks up and smiles and goes back to her seam. The old man, who has told his stories for the night, lets his eyes close where he sits, and nobody disturbs him. With the children down, the camp grows quieter, though it was never loud. The fire is fed once more. Out beyond the light, the valley waits, wide and dark and patient, and the grown-ups have the rest of the night to themselves.

With the children asleep, the talk around the fire changes. It slows down, and goes deeper. This is the hour, in camps like this, when people told the long stories: not the funny ones for the children, but the ones about where the band came from, and who the first people were, and what the animals said to one another before people learned to listen. We do not know these stories. They were never written down, and they died with the last person who told them. But we know there were stories, because there always are.

A woman is speaking now, her hands moving in the firelight. She is telling about a place three summers' walk to the south, where the water is warm and the shells are as big as your head, and where her mother's people lived before they came north. Perhaps it is true. Perhaps it grew a little in the telling. Bands like this one moved, over generations, across enormous distances, and the memory of the journey was kept in exactly this way: by the fire, out loud, in the dark.

One of the men has a flute. It is a hollow bone from the wing of a large bird, with a few holes cut along its length, and when he puts it to his lips and blows, it makes a thin, sweet, breathy note that carries surprisingly far into the night. Flutes like this, tens of thousands of years old, have been found in caves in Europe. They are among the oldest musical instruments we know. He plays a few notes, a little tune that goes up and comes down again, and then stops, and looks at it, as if surprised it still works.

Then he plays it again, and this time someone begins to hum along, and then to sing, low, a few words over and over. We cannot know the tune or the words. But it seems very unlikely that people who made flutes did not sing, and very unlikely that people who sang did not sing at night, by the fire, when the work was done. So let us say they did. Let us say it was slow, and a little sad, and that everyone knew it, and that it made the night feel smaller and warmer around them.

The old man, who has woken up, begins to speak, and the singing stops to let him. He is telling about the winter of the great snow, when he was a young man, and the band could not leave the cave for many days, and how they lived on dried meat and melted snow and the stories they told each other. He tells it slowly. He has told it many times, and every time there is a little more of it. The young hunter listens closely. One day he will tell it.

Inside, by the smaller fire, two people talk quietly so as not to wake the children. About tomorrow, mostly. Whether to go up the valley or down it. Whether the berries by the stream will last another week. Whether the old man will manage the walk if the band has to move before the snow. These were the real questions of a life like this, and they were answered the way they are still answered in most of the world: by talking them over, slowly, until everyone more or less agreed.

The man with the scratched pebble holds it up to show the woman beside him, and she takes it and turns it in the light and hands it back, and says something short and approving. He tucks it into a fold of his clothing, and will carry it for years, until it is lost, and someone will find it in the ground forty thousand years from tonight and wonder, as you might, what it meant to him. The honest answer is that we do not know. The kinder answer is that it was beautiful, and he liked it.

The talk drifts. It goes from the berries to the bear tracks to the shape of the clouds this evening, and settles, as talk does late at night, into long comfortable silences with a few words dropped into them. Nobody feels a need to fill the quiet. In a world without walls, silence was not empty. It was full of the river, and the wind in the grass, and the small sounds of the fire, and the far-off calls of animals nobody could see.

The flute player plays once more, softly, just for himself. Three notes, and a fourth, lower. Then he wraps the flute in a scrap of hide and puts it away in the pouch at his belt, where it lives. Some evenings he does not play at all. Some evenings he plays for an hour. There is nobody to please and nothing to prove, and that, perhaps, is what music was for, back at the very beginning: for the player, and for the night, and for whoever happened to be listening.

The old man has stopped talking, and his eyes are closed again, and this time nobody thinks he will open them. The woman beside him puts a fur over his shoulders, gently, and he does not stir. The fire has burned down to a bed of orange coals with a few small flames dancing over it. She feeds it a little, not much, and holds her hands out to it, and listens to the night, and lets the last of the stories settle in her mind like leaves settling on water.

Step away from the fire for a moment, out onto the grass, and look up. You have never seen a sky like this. There is no town for a thousand miles, no lamp, no glow on any horizon. The stars are not a scattering. They are a flood, from one edge of the world to the other, and the pale river of the Milky Way runs right across the middle of them, so bright it casts the faintest shadow. Two of the people have walked out to look. They do this most clear nights. It never gets old.

The man points to a bright star low in the east, and says its name. We do not know what name he used. But people all over the world, long before writing, gave the stars names and stories, and noticed that they moved in patterns, and that the patterns matched the seasons. That star rising there, in that place, at this hour, means the reindeer will be moving south soon. The sky was a calendar, and a clock, and a map, and people read it the way you read a phone.

The moon is up, a little more than half, riding above the mountains. In its light you can see the shapes of the peaks, and the pale line of the river, and the darker mass of the forest at the valley's end. A camp like this did not sleep in the pitch dark, most nights. The moon and the stars gave light enough to walk by, and to see a shape moving, and to find the way back to the fire. Moonless nights were different. On moonless nights, you stayed close.

The woman has sat down on a rock with a child who has woken and wandered out to find her. She is showing the child the sky. Not teaching, exactly. Just looking, and pointing, and saying the names. That group there, like a little bowl. That bright one that does not twinkle. The child is listening with the deep seriousness of the very tired, and will remember none of it, and all of it. In a few years she will be the one pointing.

Something streaks across the sky and is gone. A shooting star. The man's head turns to follow it, and he says a word under his breath. People have been startled by falling stars for as long as there have been people, and have told each other what they mean, and have all been wrong, and it has not mattered. He watches the place where it vanished for a while, in case there is another. There is not. He turns back toward the fire.

Back at the fire, she tells the others about the falling star, and there is a brief discussion of what it might mean, which goes nowhere, comfortably. Then someone mentions that the moon will be full in a few nights, and that is more practical. A full moon meant light for travelling, and for hunting animals that came out at night, and it meant the band could be up and busy after dark if it needed to be. Their whole month was measured this way, from full moon to full moon. It still is, in some places.

The two sky-watchers walk back across the grass toward the camp. One carries a torch, though the moon is bright enough to see by, because a torch is not only for seeing. It is for being seen, by anything out here with eyes, and for being not-worth-the-trouble. Animals that had met people and their fire learned to keep their distance. Most nights, that was all the protection anyone needed. The tent hides glow faintly from inside as they pass.

The old man has woken, and is looking out from the cave at the stars over the valley. He has watched them turn all his life. He knows, because his own old people told him, that the whole sky turns slowly around one place, and that if you keep that place on your left hand as you walk, you go toward where the sun comes up. He has never been lost. Not once. He looks at the sky the way you might look at the face of an old friend.

A girl who could not sleep has dragged her fur out of the cave and lies on her back on the grass, a little way from the fire, looking straight up. Nobody stops her. The night is mild, the fire is near, and she is not the first child to do this and will not be the last. Above her the stars wheel, so slowly that you cannot see them move, only notice, later, that they have. She is asleep before she notices. Someone will carry her in.

And someone does. Her father lifts her, fur and all, and carries her back inside, and she does not stir. The sky goes on turning over the valley, over the river, over the far dark mountains and the ice beyond them. The camp is a small ring of orange light at the bottom of all that darkness, and inside the ring, the fire is fed once more, and the people who are still awake draw a little closer to it, and say very little, because there is very little that needs to be said.

Was anyone on guard? It is a fair question, in a world with cave bears and lions and hyenas, all of them bigger than the ones you know. The honest answer is that we are not sure. But it seems likely that in most camps, most nights, somebody was awake. Not marching up and down. Just sitting by the fire, feeding it, listening, the way this man is now, with his spear beside him and his eyes on the dark beyond the light. He is not afraid. He is paying attention. There is a difference.

And he is not alone. Curled at the edge of the firelight, nose on paws, is a wolf. Or something between a wolf and a dog, because the line between them was only beginning to be drawn in this age. Some of the very first dogs may have come from wolves that learned to follow human camps for scraps, and then to sleep near the fire, and then to be useful. This one lifts its head when the man moves, and lowers it again. Its ears are better than his. If something comes, it will know first.

Once in the night the man gets up, takes the torch, and walks the edge of the camp. He is checking the things that need checking. The hides on their frame, which a fox would happily chew. The water bags. The stack of firewood. The dark place under the trees where the ground slopes down to the river, because that is the way an animal would come. Nothing moves. He stands for a while with the torch, letting whatever is out there see it, and then walks back.

A woman has woken and come out to sit with him, and they talk in low voices about the bear tracks by the stream. Old, he thinks. A day old at least. Going away from here, not toward. She agrees. Bears mostly wanted nothing to do with people, and a fire and a crowd of voices was usually enough to convince one to go elsewhere. Mostly. There were nights, in every band's memory, when mostly had not been enough. Those nights became stories too, and were told carefully, so that nobody forgot what to do.

The wolf-dog gets up, turns around twice, and lies down again facing the other way. The man watches it do this, and relaxes a little more. Animals tell you things, if you watch them. A wolf that sleeps is a wolf that has heard nothing worth waking for. In the deep quiet, the man can hear the river, and the wind moving the grass, and an owl somewhere down the valley, and, very faintly and very far away, the low grunting call of something large that is not coming any closer.

He eats a strip of dried fish from the rack, slowly, to pass the time, and because being awake makes you hungry. Keeping watch was not a hardship, exactly. It was a quiet hour with the fire and your own thoughts, and a great many people, then and now, would call that a luxury. When he grows too tired, he will wake somebody else, or he will not, and simply lie down, and trust the fire and the wolf and the general good luck that has kept the band alive this long.

Inside, the others sleep. Not in rows, and not each in their own bed. They sleep the way people slept for most of human history: close together, in a heap, children in the middle, adults around the edge, furs over the top of everybody. It was warmer this way, and safer, and it was simply how things were. A child who woke in the night found a warm back to press against and went back to sleep. Nobody, in this world, ever slept alone if they could help it.

The small fire inside the cave is fed by whoever wakes and notices it is low. That is the other kind of keeping watch, the kind nobody was assigned: you wake, you see the coals are dim, you reach out and push a branch onto them, and you sleep again. Over a night, a dozen people might do this a dozen times without any of them quite remembering it in the morning. And so the fire never went out, and nobody, exactly, kept it going.

The watcher stands at the edge of the grass one more time and looks at the sky. The moon has crossed a good part of it. He does not count hours, but he knows the shape of a night, and this one is about half gone. It is the deepest, stillest part, when even the animals seem to sleep, and the air is coldest, and the stars are brightest, and a person alone by a fire can feel, for a while, like the only person in the world.

Then he lies down where he is, at the mouth of the cave, between the fire and the dark, with the wolf-dog a few feet away and his spear beside him, and pulls a fur up over his shoulder. He does not decide to sleep. Nobody does. He watches the coals for a while, and then he is not watching them, and the night goes on without him, quite safely, as it has done ten thousand times before.

Let us stay with the sleepers for a while. There is not much to see, and that is the point. The small fire glows. The furs rise and fall. Someone murmurs and turns over. Sleep, in a camp like this, was not the eight-hour block you were taught to aim for. People went down when the dark and the tiredness came together, which was early by your standards. And they woke, many of them, somewhere in the middle of the night, for a while, and then slept again until the light.

Historians have found, in old letters and diaries from long before electric light, that people spoke of a first sleep and a second sleep, with a quiet, wakeful hour between them. Whether Ice Age people slept the same way we cannot know. But it would not be surprising. A man sits up now, in the middle of the night, not because anything woke him, but because his first sleep is done. He looks at the fire. He is not troubled. He is simply awake.

He feeds the fire, quietly, pushing the ends of the branches in toward the heart of it. He does it without thinking, the way you might pull a blanket up. Then he sits and watches the flames take hold, and listens to the others breathing. His wife is asleep beside him, one arm flung out over the child. Her breath is slow and even. He sits for a long time doing nothing at all, and there is no better word for it than peace.

Out at the cave mouth, the watcher is asleep, and his fire has burned lower, and the wolf-dog has moved a little closer to it. The stars have wheeled on. The bright one the man pointed at earlier is high now. Nobody is watching it. There is no need. It will be there tomorrow night, and the night after, and it will still be there, more or less, when your great-grandchildren look up. The valley is silent under it.

A woman wakes, and lies still, and listens. It is the listening of a mother, half asleep and half not, checking the sounds of the night against the sounds she expects. The fire is right. The breathing is right. The wolf-dog, out front, is quiet. Somewhere far off, the river. She lets her eyes close again. She will do this several times before morning, and remember none of it. It is the most ordinary thing in the world, and it kept a great many children alive.

The old man is awake too, and the two of them, the old man and the younger, talk for a little while in the low voices of the middle of the night. About nothing much. About the old man's father, who was a great one for finding honey. About whether the ache in the old man's knee means rain. These are the conversations that happened in the wakeful hour, in the dark, when the day's business was far away and there was nothing to do but be alive together. Then the old man lies back down.

The younger man gets up and takes a burning stick out to the front fire, which has burned very low, and coaxes it back. The wolf-dog opens one eye. The watcher does not wake. The man crouches there for a while in the orange light, looking out at the moonlit grass, at the shapes of the tents, at the slope beyond where the deer were this evening. Nothing moves. He has never in his life seen a night that was empty. But this one is quiet, and quiet is enough.

He comes back in, and lies down, and the second sleep takes him quickly. Now the whole cave sleeps. The small fire, fed, will last until the grey light. The painted horse stands on the wall above them all, its red earth catching a little of the glow. Forty thousand years from tonight, people will find this cave, and the ash of this fire, and the bones of this evening's fish, and they will work out, very roughly, what happened here. But they will not know how it felt. You do, a little, now.

Outside, the deer that got away has come down to the river to drink, with two others. They stand in the moonlight with the water round their feet and lift their heads, all three, at the same moment, to look at the faint glow of the fire on the hillside. Then they drink again. They have shared this valley with people for a long time, and have learned exactly how far away is far enough. The hunter, asleep, does not dream of them. He will find their tracks in the morning.

And the night goes on. The fire at the cave mouth settles into a low, red, breathing glow. The wolf-dog sighs. The watcher sleeps with his hand on his spear, and does not need it. The moon slides down toward the mountains. If you are still awake, you do not need to be. There is nothing left to watch tonight, and nothing left to do. The people are safe, and warm, and together, and so, for now, are you.

It is the coldest hour now, the one before the sky begins to pale. Even in a mild season the cold comes down hard in these hours, and a woman who has woken to feed the fire sits with her arms wrapped round herself and her shoulders up around her ears. This is the Ice Age. The world is a good deal colder than yours, and the nights are the coldest part of it. She feeds the fire a little more than she needs to, and does not feel guilty about it.

The sleepers do not feel it much. That is the point of sleeping in a heap. A dozen bodies under a dozen furs make a warmth that no single sleeper could make alone, and the children, in the middle, are the warmest of all. People in cold places all over the world have slept this way for as long as there have been people, and many still do. The idea of a room of your own, with nobody in it but you, would have seemed to these people not luxurious, but strange, and a little sad, and mostly just cold.

The woman by the fire picks up the hood she was sewing earlier and works on it a little, because her hands are cold and sewing warms them. The clothes these people wore were remarkable. Fitted trousers, and boots, and hooded jackets, sewn from hides with the fur turned inward, the seams closed tight with sinew. We know because the needles and the awls survive, and the beads that were sewn to the clothes, in rows, still lie in the ground where the clothes rotted away around them.

In the deep of winter, nights like this one were another thing altogether. Picture it, a few months on: snow on the ground, the river frozen at its edges, the band walking in from a day's hunting with the light already going at mid-afternoon. On nights like that, everything was about the fire, and the shelter, and the furs. Nobody sat out under the stars. The tents were pitched inside the cave mouth, one shelter inside another, and the fire burned between them all night long.

The old man knows winter nights. He has lived through fifty of them, and he carries the cold in his knees. On the worst nights of his life, the band did not sleep so much as wait, close around the fire, feeding it and dozing and feeding it again, until the grey light came. But most winter nights were not the worst nights. Most were simply long, and dark, and quiet, and spent under a great weight of fur with the fire glowing red at the edge of sight. He rather liked them.

Tonight, though, the cold is only the ordinary cold of the small hours, and a fire and a fur are enough. The woman holds her hands to the flames and turns them over and holds them again, and the warmth creeps up her wrists. She is thinking about nothing at all. It is a good state to be in. She will stay by the fire for a while yet, because someone should, and because it is pleasant, and then she will go back in to the warm heap and the soft breathing.

Out on the grass, frost has begun to form. Each blade carries a thin white edge that will be gone an hour after sunrise. The tents stand dark and still. Somewhere beyond them, a fox is working along the line of the river, quick and quiet, and finds nothing, and goes on. The fire on the hillside is the only warm thing for miles, and every living creature in the valley knows exactly where it is.

The girl's father wakes and sees that the small fire has burned down, and reaches out from under the furs and pushes a branch into it, and lies back. It flares. The girl, asleep beside him, frowns in her sleep and turns her face away from the light, and he moves the fur so it shades her, and she is still again. He lies and watches the shadows of the fire move on the cave roof. Then he closes his eyes, and the shadows go on moving without him.

The woman at the front fire looks up. The sky has changed. It is not lighter yet, not really. But the stars in the east have begun to lose a little of their sharpness, and the air has that particular stillness that comes just before a morning. The wolf-dog has noticed too. Its ears are up, though its head is still on its paws. It is listening to the birds, which have not begun yet, but will. It can hear them thinking about it.

She feeds the fire one last time, properly, so that it will last until the others are up. Then she sits a moment longer with her hands out to it. The cold has gone out of her fingers. The night is nearly done, and it has been a good one: no alarms, no sickness, no bear at the rubbish heap, no crying child that could not be settled. Just the fire, and the stars, and the long, slow, ordinary hours of an Ice Age night. She yawns, and pulls the fur closer, and goes in to sleep.

Close your eyes for this part, if they are not closed already, and just listen. A night like this one was never silent. It was full of small sounds, and the people who slept through it knew every one of them, the way you know the sounds of your own house: which are nothing, and which are worth waking for. Almost all of them were nothing. Let us go through them, slowly, one at a time, the way a sleeper hears them.

First, and always, the fire. A small fire makes a great many sounds. There is the low, steady breath of it, which you stop hearing after a while. There is the tick and click of the wood as it dries and splits in the heat. Now and then a branch settles and sends up a soft rush of sparks, with a sound like someone sighing. And under all of it, if you listen closely, a faint whisper, like paper, as the air moves through the coals.

Then the river. It is a little way off, down the slope, but on a still night it fills the whole valley. It does not roar. It talks, quietly and without stopping, over the stones at the shallows, a sound made of a thousand tiny sounds that never quite repeat. People who lived by rivers slept to this all their lives, and when they moved away from one, they missed it, and slept badly for a while. You may find you are the same.

The wind, when there is any. Tonight there is almost none. But even the little there is moves through the grass with a long, soft hush, and stirs the hide of the tents so that they creak, once, and are quiet. In the trees down by the water, the leaves turn over and settle. These are the sounds a sleeper checks against without knowing it. Grass. Tent. Leaves. All as they should be. Sleep on.

And the breathing. Twenty or thirty people asleep in a cave make a sound all of their own, slow and layered and not quite in time, like the sea. Somebody snores. Somebody murmurs, and stops. A child sighs in a dream. To a sleeper in the heap, this was the safest sound in the world: everyone here, everyone breathing, nobody gone. If it changed, they would wake. It does not change. It goes on, rising and falling, all through the night.

The wolf-dog makes sounds too. A sigh as it settles. The small thump of its tail once against the ground, at something in a dream. A long yawn that ends in a faint whine. And, every so often, a silence, which is the most important sound it makes: the sound of an animal lifting its head and listening. Then the head goes down again, and the tail thumps, and whatever it was, it was nothing.

Further off, the night animals. An owl, down the valley, calling and waiting and calling again, and never getting an answer. A fox barking, once, sharp and strange, a long way away. The far, low sound of something large moving through the grass beyond the river, unhurried, minding its own business. And once, so faint you might have imagined it, the cry of a bird flying over in the dark, going somewhere, high up, alone.

Then the sounds of the camp itself, which are the sounds of people being alive. A cough. A fur being pulled up. The scrape of someone shifting on the grass bed. A few words, mumbled, and an answer that is not really an answer. Someone getting up, and the soft pad of feet on stone, and a pause, and the feet coming back. The sound of the fire being fed, which is a particular sound, a soft crunch and then a quickening in the breath of the flames.

And under all of these, and around them, the silence of the stone. A cave has a sound of its own, which is the sound of nothing happening in a large, still, enclosed place. It softens everything. It makes the fire sound closer and the river sound further. Children who grew up in caves like this knew that sound better than they knew their own names, and it meant one thing to them, and one thing only, and that thing was home.

That is the whole of it. Fire, river, wind, breathing, the dog, the owl, the small sounds of people, and the great soft silence of the stone. Nothing else. Nothing that needs you. If your own house makes its own small sounds tonight, let them be these. Let the fridge be the river, and the traffic be the wind, and whoever is breathing near you be the heap in the cave. Everyone is here. Everyone is breathing. Nobody is gone. Sleep on.

While they sleep, let us look a little further than the firelight. This valley, with its river and its cave and its herds, is one small place in a very large world, and the people asleep in it know only a corner of that world. To the north, beyond the mountains, the ice begins: a wall of it, in places a mile high, that has stood there for longer than anyone's stories go back. The wind that comes down off it is the reason for the furs, and the fire, and the hoods.

To the south and east, where the land is open, the herds move. Reindeer and horses in their thousands, wild cattle bigger than any bull you have seen, and the mammoths, in small family groups, moving slowly across the grass under the moon. The mammoths do not fear anything in this valley, not even the people. They are too big. The people follow them at a distance, and pick up what they leave, and very occasionally, when everything goes right, they bring one down, and eat for a month.

A few days' walk to the west, the land ends at the sea, and other bands live there, on the beaches and the cliffs, eating shellfish and seals and the fish that come in on the tide. The band in our cave knows them. They meet, some years, in the summer, at a place both bands remember, and they trade shells for flint, and stories for stories, and sometimes a young man or a young woman goes home with the other band, and that is how the world stays knitted together.

Nobody in the cave knows how many people there are in the world. Not many, by your standards. If you had gathered every human being alive on this night and walked them past the fire, it would have taken a while, but not for ever. Perhaps as many as live in one large city today. Perhaps fewer. They were spread thin across a wide, cold, empty world, in bands like this one, each band knowing a few others, each one keeping its fire.

There were also, in this age, other kinds of people. Not long before this night, in the way that an old man counts time, the last of the Neanderthals were living in valleys like this one, to the south and west. The people in our cave may have heard stories of them. Some of the people in our cave may carry a little of them, in the way their brows are shaped, or their shoulders. We do. A small part of most of us, tonight, comes from them.

The old man, asleep, is a library. Everything the band knows that is not in someone's hands is in his head: where the flint comes from, which plants heal and which kill, what the sky does before a storm, the names of people who died before the children were born, the whole long story of how the band came to this valley. When he dies, some of it will die with him. Some he has already told. That is why he tells it so often, and why the children are made to listen.

Somewhere out in the dark, far down the valley, another fire is burning. If you stood on the slope above the cave you might just see it, a spark of orange at the bottom of the night. Another band, camped by the same river. The people in the cave know they are there. They will meet, in a few days, and there will be talk, and perhaps an argument about the berries, and it will be settled. Tonight, each band keeps its own fire, and the valley holds them both.

It is easy, looking back across forty thousand years, to think of these people as somehow less than us. They were not. Their brains were the size of yours. They made music and pictures and jokes. They loved their children and argued with their neighbours and lay awake worrying about the winter. Put a child from that cave in a house in your street and she would grow up to drive a car and complain about the internet. The only difference between them and you is what they knew, and when they were born.

And the ice, to the north, is very slowly beginning to melt. Not tonight. Not for thousands of years yet. But the long winter that has gripped the world for as long as anyone's stories run is, somewhere far off, beginning to loosen. The people in the cave will never know it. Their children's children's children, a great many generations on, will walk into a warmer world, and plant seeds, and build walls, and eventually, one night, lie in a bed in a lit room and listen to a story about a cave.

But that is far away, and it is late, and the cave is quiet. Whatever the world is doing out there, in here it is warm, and the fire is fed, and everyone who should be asleep is asleep. The painted horse keeps its watch on the wall. The wolf-dog keeps its watch at the door. And the night keeps on, slow and dark and safe, toward a morning that is still a long way off.

The old man has woken once more, in the way of old men, and sits with his back to the rock and his fur round his shoulders, watching the small fire. He is not going to sleep again for a while, and he does not mind. Let us sit with him, and think about what a man like this knew. Not facts, the way you know facts. Things. Hundreds of plants, by leaf and root and smell, and what each was good for. The tracks of every animal in the valley, and how old a track was, and which way the animal was going, and whether it was hurt.

He knew the river the way you know your own street. Where it was shallow enough to cross, and in which months. Where the fish gathered, and when. Which bends flooded in spring, and which bank a bear liked to fish from, and so was best avoided. None of this was written anywhere. It lived in his head, and in the heads of a few dozen other people, and it was passed on by walking the river with a child and pointing, and saying the names, and going back the next year and saying them again.

He knew the animals. Not as things to eat, though they were that. As neighbours. He knew that the mammoths came through the valley twice a year, and that they mourned their dead, standing round a fallen one for days. He knew that reindeer could smell you from a mile off if the wind was wrong, and that horses could not. He knew which birds cried out when a lion was near, and had trusted those birds with his life more than once, and had been right to.

The women knew all this too, and more of some of it. A woman in the band might know two hundred plants and their seasons, and where each grew, and which part to use, and how to prepare it so it did not make you ill. The roots that were cooking earlier had to be cooked; raw, they would have twisted your stomach for a day. Someone learned that once, the hard way, a very long time ago, and told everyone, and it was never forgotten. That, more than the spears, is what kept these people alive.

What did they not know? A great deal, by your measure. They did not know what the stars were, or why the ice was there, or what was on the other side of the sea. They did not know what caused a fever, or why a child was born wrong, or where people went when they died, though they had stories about all of these, and the stories were a comfort. They lived, in some ways, in a world of enormous mystery. They also lived in a world they understood, in its details, better than most of us understand our own.

And they knew how to make things. Not a few things: everything. Every object in this camp was made by someone in it, from something found within a day's walk. The clothes, the tools, the bags, the beds, the fire itself. If a thing broke, the person who broke it could usually mend it, and if not, someone sitting nearby could. Try to imagine, for a moment, being able to make with your own hands every single object you own. They could. It was not remarkable to them. It was Tuesday.

A mother, half awake, moves the fur off a sleeping child who has grown too warm, and settles again. She knows things too, that no one wrote down and no one will: how to quiet a crying baby in the dark without waking the others, which berries are safe for a child with a loose stomach, how to tell from a child's breathing whether it is sleeping or pretending. This knowledge does not leave a mark in the ground. It is the oldest knowledge there is, and it is still being passed on, tonight, in houses everywhere.

The old man has come out to the front fire now, slowly, on his stiff knees, and sits looking out at the valley under the last of the stars. He is thinking, perhaps, about the boy he taught to make a spear point this evening. Or about his own father, who taught him. Or about nothing at all, which is a fine thing to think about in the small hours. The wolf-dog gets up and comes to lie beside him, and he puts a hand on its rough back, and they sit there together, two old animals by a fire.

Perhaps the most important thing he knew was this: that the band would go on. He had seen bad winters and hungry summers, and children lost, and the band was still here. The young hunter would be a good hunter. The girl who spilled the water would one day know the river as well as he did. The stories would be told. He had no word for the future, but he trusted it, the way you trust the sun to come up, because it always had. He feeds the fire, and warms his hands, and yawns.

Then he goes back in and lies down among the others, and pulls the fur up, and is asleep almost at once, the way the very old and the very young can be. The small fire glows on. Above it, the painted horse runs, forever, across its wall. Everything the old man knows is safe for tonight, inside his sleeping head, and inside the heads of the others, and in the hands of the boy who made his first flake this evening and is holding it still, in his sleep, in his fist.

We are in the last hour of the night now, the one that belongs to nobody. Everyone in the cave is asleep, even the watcher, even the old man. The fire at the cave mouth has burned down to a bed of coals with one small flame walking back and forth across it. The wolf-dog sleeps with its nose under its tail. The moon has gone behind the mountains. There is nothing to do, and no one to do it, and the night is holding its breath.

Down at the river, the deer have gone. The water goes on without them, murmuring over the stones, the way it did before there were deer, or people, or a valley. Mist has begun to gather over it in the cold, thin and white, lying along the surface like a second, slower river. In an hour, the first light will find it and turn it gold. Nobody will see that happen. The people will be asleep, and the deer will be far up the slope, and only the fox, going home, will notice.

Inside, the heap of sleepers has shifted in the night, the way it does. A child has rolled toward the fire and been rolled back, by someone who does not remember doing it. A fur has slid off a shoulder and been pulled up again. Someone is snoring, gently. Someone else has an arm across someone else's face, and neither of them minds. This is what safety looked like, for most of the time there have been people. Not a locked door. A warm heap, and a fire, and everyone you knew within reach.

The watcher half-wakes, feels the cold on his face, reaches out without opening his eyes, and pushes the last of the branches onto the coals. They catch. The little flame grows for a moment into a proper fire, and the light of it moves on the rock above him, and on his closed eyes, and he is already asleep again. It will burn now until the others rise. The wood pile is empty. Someone will fill it tomorrow. That is tomorrow's business.

Out on the grass the frost is complete now, white on every blade, and the tents stand pale in it. There is not a breath of wind. In this stillness, sound carries a very long way: the river, an owl far down the valley, and the tiny tick of the fire on the hillside. If you stood out here you would see the eastern sky beginning, just barely, to separate itself from the mountains. Not light. Just less dark. The stars over there are going out one by one, quietly, like people leaving a room.

The old man sleeps on his side with his knees drawn up, the way he has slept since he was a boy. He is dreaming, perhaps. We do not know what these people dreamed of, but it seems certain that they dreamed, and told each other their dreams in the morning, and wondered about them. He will wake with the light, and be stiff, and complain a little, and then get up and go out to look at the day, and tell somebody what kind of day it will be. He is usually right.

And the night keeps going, a little longer. It has nearly done its work. It has rested the hunter's legs and the flint worker's hands and the old man's knees. It has let the children grow, a little, the way children do in their sleep. It has kept the fire, and been kept by it. Forty thousand years from now, someone lying in the dark will listen to a story about it and feel, for a moment, the warmth of that fire on their face. That is you. That is now. It worked.

There is nothing more to see tonight. The fire is fed. The cave is warm. The people are safe and asleep, all of them, in their heap under the painted horse, and the wolf-dog is asleep at the door, and the valley is quiet from the river to the ice. Let your own breathing slow to match theirs. Let the pillow take your head, the way the grass takes theirs. You have walked a long way today too, whatever your day was. You are allowed to stop.

The small fire glows red. The furs rise and fall. Somewhere a long way off, the first bird thinks about singing, and decides to wait a little longer. The painted horse runs on its wall. The coals tick and settle. And the night, which has been very long and very kind, goes on a little longer still, for them, and for you, in the warm dark, with nothing left to do but sleep. Goodnight.
